title.en: The earliest names of Pune: competing accounts

summary.en: Encyclopaedia accounts link Pune to early inscriptions that call the area Punaka or Punya vishaya, but they disagree about the dates and the dynasty. PunePedia has not yet read the inscriptions themselves.

en.text: The English Wikipedia article on the history of Pune says that two copper plates dated 758 and 768 CE, issued by the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I, refer to the area as 'Puny Vishaya' and 'Punaka Vishaya'. It supports this with an article by M. R. Kantak in the Bulletin of the Deccan College Research Institute.

The article on Pune on the same site attributes plates of 758 and 768 CE to the Yadava dynasty instead. It also mentions plates of 858 and 868 CE naming an agricultural settlement called Punnaka, and a Rashtrakuta inscription of 937 CE naming Punya-vishaya. Most of these statements carry no visible footnote.

Because the two accounts disagree on the dynasty and the dates, no single 'first name' or founding date is presented here as settled. The next step is to read the plate texts in a published edition and record the exact readings.

summary.en: Identify every inscription said to name Pune, find its published edition, and record the exact wording, date, issuing ruler and page reference.

en.text: Leads to follow: M. R. Record each plate separately, including any where scholars read the place name differently.

title.en: Research lead: when was the Pataleshwar cave cut?

summary.en: The cave is commonly dated to the 8th century and the Rashtrakuta period, but the source consulted does not tie that date to a specific reference.

en.text: The encyclopaedia article consulted gives an 8th-century, Rashtrakuta-period date but does not attach it to a particular footnote. Check the architectural surveys it cites (Fergusson and Burgess 1880, pp. 426–427; Sinclair 1877) and the Archaeological Survey of India's records before placing the cave on the public timeline.

title.en: Pune razed, then made the home of Jijabai and Shivaji

summary.en: In 1630–31 a Bijapur general razed Pune. Shahaji later chose the town as the residence of Jijabai and the young Shivaji.

en.text: Murar Jagdeo, a general of the Adil Shahi kingdom of Bijapur, razed Pune in 1630–31; the account cited says he had donkey-drawn ploughs run over the ground.
Shahaji, who held Pune as part of his jagir, later chose it as the residence of his wife Jijabai and their son Shivaji.
Both scholarly sources are known here only through the encyclopaedia page that cites them. Read them directly before this entry is reviewed.

title.en: Shaniwar Wada is founded

summary.en: Peshwa Bajirao I laid the foundation of Shaniwar Wada on a Saturday in January 1730; the opening ceremony followed two years later.

en.text: The foundation was laid on Saturday, 10 January 1730, by Peshwa Bajirao I, and the opening ceremony took place on 22 January 1732.
Uday S. Kulkarni's history of the period names some of the craftsmen who worked on it, among them Shivaram Krishna Khasgiwale, Devaji Sutar and Kondaji Sutar.
The 1885 Poona Gazetteer's account of the city should be added here with page numbers.

title.en: The Devdeveshwar temple on Parvati is completed

summary.en: The main temple on Parvati hill was completed under Peshwa Balaji Bajirao in 1749, and a gold pinnacle was added in 1760.

en.text: The Devdeveshwar temple was completed under Balaji Bajirao in 1749; a gold pinnacle was added in 1760.
A widely told account connects the temple complex to Kashibai's recovery from a leg ailment after a vow at an older Devi shrine on the hill.

title.en: Mahadji Shinde's last rites at Wanwadi

summary.en: Mahadji Shinde was cremated at Wanwadi in 1794, beside a Shiva temple he had built. A memorial was added there in 1910.

en.text: Mahadji Shinde died in 1794; his cremation took place on 12 February 1794 on the grounds of a Shiva temple he had built at Wanwadi.
In 1910 a samadhi was built at the cremation spot, commissioned by Maharaja Madho Rao Scindia of Gwalior and designed by the Bombay firm of Shapurjee N. Chandabhoy.

title.en: The Battle of Khadki and the fall of Pune

summary.en: On 5 November 1817 East India Company troops defeated a Maratha army at Khadki. Twelve days later the Company took over Shaniwar Wada.

en.text: The Battle of Khadki (also called Kirkee or Ganeshkhind) was fought on 5 November 1817 between a Maratha force under Bapu Gokhale and East India Company troops under Lieutenant-Colonel Charles Burr, and ended in a Company victory.
The Company took over Shaniwar Wada on 17 November 1817.
Peshwa rule ended in 1818 with the defeat of Bajirao II.
The encyclopaedia page is inconsistent in places (one reference gives the year as 1816). Troop strengths and casualty figures are left out until checked against a primary account.

title.en: The Hindoo College opens — later Deccan College

summary.en: On 6 October 1821 the Hindoo College, also known as the Poona Sanskrit College, was established. It later became Deccan College.

en.text: The college was established on 6 October 1821 as the Hindoo College under Mountstuart Elphinstone, using money from the former Peshwa's Dakshina fund.

The college is described as first meeting in Vishrambaug Wada and later moving to its present campus; the foundation stone of the new building is dated 15 October 1864 and the move to 23 March 1868. These statements are not footnoted on the page consulted.

en.text: Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls at Bhide Wada, Budhwar Peth, in 1848.

title.en: Jyotirao Phule founds the Satyashodhak Samaj

summary.en: On 24 September 1873 Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune to oppose caste privilege and widen education and rights.

en.text: The Satyashodhak Samaj was founded in Pune on 24 September 1873 by Jyotirao Phule. Savitribai Phule led its women's section.

Its aims included education and greater social and political rights for women, peasants and Dalits; rejection of caste hierarchy and of priestly intermediaries; and simpler weddings, inter-caste marriage, widow remarriage and an end to child marriage.

title.en: Fergusson College is founded

summary.en: The Deccan Education Society, formed in 1884, established Fergusson College in 1885.

en.text: The Deccan Education Society was formed in 1884 and established Fergusson College in 1885. Its founders included V. S. Apte, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Vishnushastri Chiplunkar, Mahadeo Ballal Namjoshi and Gopal Ganesh Agarkar. The college was named after Sir James Fergusson, then Governor of Bombay.

title.en: Who started Pune's public Ganeshotsav?

summary.en: Pune's public Ganesh festival began in the early 1890s, but who started it, and in which year, is still argued over. In 2017 the question became a public dispute.

en.text: In 2017 the Pune Municipal Corporation prepared to mark 125 years of the community Ganesh festival, crediting Bal Gangadhar Tilak and the year 1893.

The Shrimant Bhausaheb Rangari Ganapati Trust argued that Bhausaheb Laxman Jawale, known as Bhau Rangari, organised the first public celebration in 1892, with three idols installed in different parts of the city. It said Tilak's own first public idol came in 1894, and cited a government reference book on freedom fighters.
The then mayor, a descendant of Tilak, held to 1893 and Tilak's role in encouraging public participation, citing J. S. Karandikar's 1957 history of the festival among other evidence.
A historian quoted in the same report suggested that police permission records from 1892–93 could settle the question. PunePedia has not seen those records.

title.en: The Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute is founded

summary.en: BORI was founded on 6 July 1917 in honour of R. G. Bhandarkar. Two years later it began its critical edition of the Mahabharata.

en.text: The decision to found the institute was taken at a meeting in Pune on 6 July 1915, and it was founded on 6 July 1917 to honour Sir Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar.

The Government of Bombay's manuscript collection was transferred to the institute on 1 April 1918. Work on the critical edition of the Mahabharata was inaugurated on 1 April 1919, and its completion was announced on 22 September 1966 by President Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan.

title.en: The Poona Pact is signed at Yerwada

summary.en: After Gandhi began a fast in Yerwada Central Jail, an agreement on the representation of the Depressed Classes was signed there on 24 September 1932.

en.text: Gandhi, imprisoned at Yerwada, began a fast on 20 September 1932 against the separate electorates for the Depressed Classes in the Communal Award.

The Poona Pact was signed at Yerwada Central Jail on 24 September 1932. B. R. Ambedkar signed for the Depressed Classes and Madan Mohan Malaviya for the Hindus. It replaced separate electorates with reserved seats within joint electorates.
The number of reserved seats is stated inconsistently on the page consulted and is left out until checked against the pact's text.

title.en: Gandhi's imprisonment at the Aga Khan Palace

summary.en: Arrested at the start of the Quit India movement, Gandhi was held at the Aga Khan Palace until May 1944. Mahadev Desai and Kasturba Gandhi died there.

en.text: Gandhi was arrested early on 9 August 1942, after the Quit India movement was launched, and was held at the Aga Khan Palace until his release on health grounds on 6 May 1944.
Mahadev Desai died there on 15 August 1942, aged 50, and Kasturba Gandhi on 22 February 1944, aged 74.

title.en: The Panshet dam fails and Pune floods

summary.en: On 12 July 1961, in its first year of storing water, the Panshet dam gave way and floodwater swept into Pune.

en.text: The Panshet dam failed on 12 July 1961, during its first year of storage, causing major flooding in Pune. The Khadakwasla dam downstream was also damaged.
The account consulted attributes the failure to a conduit through the earthen dam built from plain concrete blocks instead of reinforced concrete, because of a shortage of steel.
Death-toll estimates vary and are left out until an official inquiry report is consulted.
